metadata.title: The 402-Line Prompt: How Decomposition Makes Agents 5x Faster
metadata.purpose: Take one real slow-agent case apart in the Teardown register: explain why cutting a 402-line prompt makes agents faster instead of dumber. Land the design philosophy — just-in-time knowledge loading — as the carry-out. Nbb cut of the cwc-workshops hai-simple reel; same question and same case, machinery explained and design judged.
metadata.anchor_pair: S03 -> S09 (must be the SAME case: 402-line/12-tool low-stock sweep)
metadata.one_flag: S08 — measured on one workflow, not a guaranteed multiplier

beats.narration_text: Slow agent, so you add more tools, more context, more instructions — that's the obvious move. It's the opposite. Why does cutting a 402-line prompt make agents five times faster?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types the naive fix, hesitates on 'more', corrects to 'fewer', lands the real question

props.text:
My agent has 12 tools
and a 402-line prompt.
Just add more tools?
Why does cutting it make agents faster?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md. Narration is 30 words + lead_silence_s 0.8, giving the typing a >9s window (TIMING LAW). VERIFY media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the more->fewer correction is visible before compiling further.

beats.narration_text: The agent works. That's the setup. What's actually happening is that every call runs longer and costs more than the work being done.

shot.new_visual_element: Agent box, clock ticking up, cost ticking up

production_viz.label: It works. But it's slow.
production_viz.mechanic: An 'AGENT' box in bold INK, center. Below it two readouts tick upward: a clock icon with seconds climbing, and a cost figure climbing, both in crimson. The climbing numerals are the beat's only crimson element.

beats.narration_text: The natural reading is scarcity: pack more in. More tools, more context, more lines in the system prompt so it never misses a case. That's how you'd fix an underperforming tool — give it more to work with.

shot.new_visual_element: ADD MORE — tools, context, instructions stacking up

production_viz.label: ADD MORE — the natural reading
production_viz.mechanic: Large 'ADD MORE' heading in bold INK. Below, three labels stack upward one at a time: 'more tools', 'more context', 'more instructions'. Sell this as reasonable. No crimson — this beat is the wrong guess, not the break.

beats.narration_text: Hold one case. A 402-line prompt, 12 tools, one task — a daily low-stock sweep. Here's what actually happened on that run: 102 tool calls, 488 seconds.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — 402 lines / 12 tools / low-stock sweep case card

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — the low-stock sweep
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A case card in serif: '402 LINES' and '12 TOOLS' at top in INK, 'LOW-STOCK SWEEP' beneath, then '102 tool calls' and '488 seconds' in large crimson numerals at bottom. One crimson underline beneath the seconds figure. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS AT B09.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Every one of those 402 lines gets fed into the model on every call. All 12 tools sit in the model's attention on every call, even when only one of them applies. More isn't the problem. Carrying all of it, always, is.

shot.new_visual_element: All 402 lines / 12 tools loaded on EVERY call, one used

production_viz.label: Read every time, used once
production_viz.mechanic: A tall block of 402 small INK lines on the left, all highlighted at once each call. On the right, 12 tool icons all lit, then 11 dim to grey and 1 stays crimson-lit — 'used once'. 'CARRYING ALL OF IT, ALWAYS' label in crimson beneath.

beats.narration_text: Three levers, each trading a different thing. Tools are stateless calls — the model asks a question, gets an answer back, then decides what to do next. Skills are instruction blocks that load into context only when the model needs them, not before. Subagents run in their own context window — a separate conversation, for a task that needs full autonomy.

production_viz.label: Three levers
production_viz.mechanic: Three columns appear in sequence, each a bold INK label over one line of description: 'TOOLS — stateless calls', 'SKILLS — loaded on demand', 'SUBAGENTS — own context window'. A single teal underline sweeps beneath each label as it lands.

beats.narration_text: So the 402-line prompt splits along one seam: what has to be there every call, and what only has to be there sometimes. The core shrinks to 15 lines — role, decision logic, output format. The rest becomes five skill modules: reorder policy, forecasting, notifications, vendor lookup, audit logging. Each loads into context only when the task actually calls for it.

shot.new_visual_element: 402 lines splits into 15-line core + 5 skill modules

production_viz.label: 402 lines -> 15-line core + 5 skills
production_viz.mechanic: The 402-line block from B04 contracts down to a small '15 LINES' core box in teal, center. Five small skill tiles fan out beneath it, each labelled: reorder policy, forecasting, notifications, vendor lookup, audit logging. Dotted connector lines from core to each tile, drawn one at a time, none lit until called.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill call actually looks like. The core issues one instruction — run the forecasting skill — and stops. On the other side of that boundary, the skill loads its own two-hundred-line sub-prompt, runs its own reasoning, and returns one result. The core never sees those two hundred lines. Complexity is still there; it's just hidden behind the interface.

shot.new_visual_element: Core -> boundary line -> skill's own sub-prompt -> one result back

production_viz.label: Complexity hides behind the interface
production_viz.mechanic: A vertical crimson boundary line splits the frame. Left: '15-LINE CORE' box sends one arrow labelled 'run forecasting skill' across the line. Right: the line crosses into a much larger 'FORECASTING SKILL — 200 LINES' block with its own small reasoning loop icon, which collapses to a single small 'RESULT' box that arrows back to the core. The boundary line is the beat's crimson accent; everything else is INK/teal.

beats.narration_text: One flag on the numbers. Five times faster, a hundred seconds — that's one team, one workflow, one measurement. How much you actually gain depends on whether your task splits cleanly into bounded pieces. That's a judgment about your workflow, not a promised multiplier from this one.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ONE FLAG — one measured workflow, not a universal multiplier

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG — one workflow's numbers
production_viz.mechanic: A crimson 'FLAG' pill label at top-right — the reel's only hedge. Centre: '5x' and '~100s' in large INK, with a small caption beneath in serif italic: 'one team, one workflow, measured'. A faint dotted question mark beside 'your task?' in teal.

beats.narration_text: Back to the sweep, same case. The task that took 102 tool calls and 488 seconds now runs as 3 scripts in about 100 seconds. Same output, same correctness — about five times faster. Nothing was made smarter; the model just stopped carrying context it didn't need.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same case card, now decomposed numbers

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — decomposed
production_viz.mechanic: THE B03 CARD RETURNS, identical layout — '402 LINES' / '12 TOOLS' / 'LOW-STOCK SWEEP' at top. But the bottom numerals are replaced: '102 -> 3 scripts' and '488s -> ~100s' in teal (was crimson at B03). A small 'SAME CORRECTNESS' label appears beneath. Teal replacing crimson marks the fix.

beats.narration_text: This works when the pieces are genuinely separable — a lookup, a policy check, a template — each bounded enough to hand off to a tool or a skill on its own. Split what already has clean seams.

shot.new_visual_element: Three bounded pieces, each cleanly boxed and handed off

production_viz.label: Bounded pieces split cleanly
production_viz.mechanic: Three small labelled boxes — 'lookup', 'policy check', 'template' — each drawn with a clean solid teal border, each with a short arrow handing off to a tool/skill icon beside it. Clean, contained, no overlap.

beats.narration_text: It fails when the task is one continuous judgment call. Splitting that just introduces a boundary the model now has to cross both ways, and the back-and-forth can cost more than the single big prompt ever did. This works if the task has seams; it fails if it doesn't.

shot.new_visual_element: Mirroring B10 — one judgment call, forced boundary, costly back-and-forth

production_viz.label: One judgment call, forced apart
production_viz.mechanic: Mirroring B10: one continuous wavy INK line representing 'one judgment call' gets a crimson boundary cut through its middle, then arrows bounce back and forth across the cut multiple times, each pass in crimson, labelled 'back-and-forth' beneath. Crimson bouncing arrows are the beat's accent.

beats.narration_text: Faster agents don't know less — they load only the knowledge each task actually needs, exactly when it needs it.

props.quote: Faster agents don't know less — they load only the knowledge each task actually needs, exactly when it needs it.
props.sparkLine: Load what it needs. When it needs it.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini today. Hand it your own agent's system prompt and it separates decision logic — how the agent decides — from domain knowledge — what it needs to know — then splits the knowledge into skills the agent can load on demand, with an estimate of the token and latency difference. Go deeper: which of your skills would actually be better as their own subagent, with its own context window? Liam, in for Bear.
